Ethics approval is typically not required for theoretical work, simulations, reviews, meta-analyses, or secondary analyses of published data.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 472 columns across 63 data files.
#### Issues Identified
2 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(File = c("prakash_vs_controls_independent_ttest_analysis.jasp", "prakash_vs_controls_independent_ttest_data.csv"), Column = c("C>G scores", "C>G scores"), Issues = c("🏷️ Problematic column name — Column name has characters not allowed in file names (\">\")", "🏷️ Problematic column name — Column name has characters not allowed in file names (\">\")" )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE) ```
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 63 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

This module also assesses whether the paper's Python code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 15 Python code files.
#### Run order

The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first) and numeric filename prefixes. Python has no `source()`-equivalent import-based ordering signal (an `import` loads a module, not the paper's own analysis flow), so that basis never applies here.

#### Execution

**The Python code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 15 scripts: 1 ran without error, 11 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 0 are written for Python 2 and not run. 3 files were not run on their own, because other files import them: faceScrub.zip/faceScrub/src/models.py (by faceScrub.zip/faceScrub/src/test_color_rotation.py, faceScrub.zip/faceScrub/src/test_performance.py, faceScrub.zip/faceScrub/src/train.py, ComputationalPartFigures.ipynb); imageNet.zip/imageNet/src/modeling/models.py (by ComputationalPartFigures.ipynb, get_maximizations.py, test_color_inverse.py, imageNet.zip/imageNet/src/modeling/test_color_rotation.py, imageNet.zip/imageNet/src/modeling/test_performance.py, imageNet.zip/imageNet/src/modeling/train.py); params.py (by imageNet.zip/imageNet/src/modeling/train.py). Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions (e.g. in a `requirements.txt`). **A script looked for 5 files in another folder than the deposit has them**, so before running it once more we copied them there: `faceScrub.zip/faceScrub/result/performance_fold0.csv` to `faceScrub.zip/result/performance_fold0.csv` for `FaceScrubFigure.ipynb`; `faceScrub.zip/faceScrub/result/performance_fold1.csv` to `faceScrub.zip/result/performance_fold1.csv` for `FaceScrubFigure.ipynb`; `faceScrub.zip/faceScrub/result/performance_fold2.csv` to `faceScrub.zip/result/performance_fold2.csv` for `FaceScrubFigure.ipynb`; `faceScrub.zip/faceScrub/result/performance_fold3.csv` to `faceScrub.zip/result/performance_fold3.csv` for `FaceScrubFigure.ipynb`; `faceScrub.zip/faceScrub/result/performance_fold4.csv` to `faceScrub.zip/result/performance_fold4.csv` for `FaceScrubFigure.ipynb`. Building paths from the top of the project (as with `here::here()`), or keeping the folders the code expects, solves this.

info.title: Color Cues, Developmental Coupling, and the Limits of the Late-Sighted Model: A Commentary on Vogelsang et al. (2024)

author.affiliation:
Fielding Graduate University
								
									Santa Barbara
									California
									USA

text.text: Précis: Vogelsang et al. (2024) attribute late-sighted patients' reliance on color to missing a luminance-first stage of infancy.
But infant color and luminance sensitivity mature together, with no such stage, and the reported group difference does not survive reanalysis on the log-odds scale.
Why do we recognize objects just as readily in grayscale as in color?
Vogelsang et al. (2024) offer a developmental answer: visual robustness to chromatic change may be a consequence of the typically immature color vision system present in human neonates.
text.formatted: <ref type="bibr">Vogelsang et al. (2024)</ref> offer a developmental answer: visual robustness to chromatic change may be a consequence of the typically immature color vision system present in human neonates.

text.text: Because infants begin life with cone photoreceptors that are markedly limited in their transduction efficiency (Yuodelis & Hendrickson, 1986), they initially experience a world that is effectively color-degraded.
text.formatted: Because infants begin life with cone photoreceptors that are markedly limited in their transduction efficiency <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">(Yuodelis & Hendrickson, 1986)</ref>, they initially experience a world that is effectively color-degraded.

text.text: This early phase of impoverished chromatic experience, on this account, forces the developing visual system to build object representations grounded in luminance rather than color, thereby conferring later resilience to chromatic removal.

The Vogelsang et al. (2024) paper is a product of this program, which has been described in overview by Sinha and Held (2012), Sinha (2013) and Gilad-Gutnick (2023) and whose cohorts have been studied across a range of visual functions (for example Gupta et al., 2022, on visual memory capacity after early-onset and extended blindness).
text.formatted: The <ref type="bibr">Vogelsang et al. (2024)</ref> paper is a product of this program, which has been described in overview by <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Sinha and Held (2012)</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Sinha (2013)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Gilad-Gutnick (2023)</ref> and whose cohorts have been studied across a range of visual functions (for example <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Gupta et al., 2022, on</ref> visual memory capacity after early-onset and extended blindness).

text.text: These late-sighted individuals, tested months or years after surgery, showed worse recognition performance for grayscale than for color images.
Normally sighted controls showed no such difference.
A second experiment confirmed that Prakash patients exhibit mature, adult-like color sensitivity within days of surgery.
Computational simulations using deep convolutional neural networks trained under different color-exposure regimens broadly supported the hypothesis.
The paper is ambitious and the empirical observations are novel.
The theoretical challenge, however, is consequential.

Substantial psychophysical and electrophysiological research, developed from the late 1980s through the 2000s, with Teller's (1997) Friedenwald Lecture providing a synthesis of the early work, establishes two related but distinct points.
text.formatted: Substantial psychophysical and electrophysiological research, developed from the late 1980s through the 2000s, with <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Teller's (1997)</ref> Friedenwald Lecture providing a synthesis of the early work, establishes two related but distinct points.

text.text: First, color sensitivity and luminance sensitivity are developmentally coupled through shared photoreceptor immaturity.

Vogelsang et al. advance a sequencing claim rather than an independence claim: their account requires a luminance-first window during which object representations are consolidated before mature color input becomes available.
The coupling evidence undermines this premise directly, by showing that the same front-end bottleneck constrains both color and luminance simultaneously, so that the window does not exist.
Second, even within the chromatic domain, different subsystems mature in a specific cascade rather than simultaneously.

On the single chromatic discrimination task they were given, the Prakash patients perform like normally sighted controls within days of surgery (Section 2.2) -a level of chromatic performance that normally developing children do not reach until adolescence.
This body of evidence bears directly on the Vogelsang et al. account.
The alternative this commentary points toward can be stated at the outset.
What distinguishes a Prakash patient at sight onset from a neonate is not that one has color vision and the other does not.

It is that the Prakash patient receives, in a single step, a visual world far more complete than anything an infant encounters: full-field patterned input, chromatic and luminance structure arriving together at near-normal contrast, delivered to a brain that already has language, mature attention, and years of tactile and auditory knowledge of objects, but no prior experience of using any of it visually.
The infant receives the opposite: a signal degraded in every dimension at once, improving slowly over years, while the representations that depend on it are still being built.
The two differ along many dimensions besides color -in acuity, contrast, field, attention, cognitive maturity, and the sheer rate at which the signal arrives.

The richness and simultaneity of the latesighted patient's first visual input, arriving when the brain is not prepared to integrate it normally, is at least as plausible a cause of their later color dependence as the absence of a colordegraded phase.
On that reading the color-specific story is epiphenomenal to a more general developmental disruption.
Sections 3.5 and 5 develop this alternative; the companion paper (Peterzell, 2026) specifies a mechanism for it.
text.formatted: Sections 3.5 and 5 develop this alternative; the companion paper <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Peterzell, 2026)</ref> specifies a mechanism for it.

text.text: >Summary of Vogelsang et al. (2024)
text.formatted: <head n="2." >Summary of Vogelsang et al. (2024)</head>

text.text: Ten Prakash patients (aged 8-26 years) and ten age-and socioeconomic-status-matched normally sighted controls named common objects presented first in grayscale and then in full color.
The key measure was the "color > gray benefit" (the difference in naming accuracy between conditions).
text.formatted: The key measure was the "color > gray benefit" (the difference in naming accuracy between conditions).

text.text: A terminological point is worth fixing here, since the two are easily conflated.
I use "grayscale" for images carrying luminance modulation alone, and "luminance" for the luminance component of a stimulus.

Natural images, and the full-color condition of this experiment, carry luminance and chromatic modulation together; the grayscale condition therefore removes chromatic modulation rather than adding luminance modulation, and a "luminance-grounded" representation is one that relies on the luminance component of a stimulus that may also contain chromatic structure.
All ten Prakash patients showed a positive benefit.
The group mean was significantly larger than that of controls, who showed no reliable difference between conditions (t(18) = 3.501, p = 0.003, d = 1.566).
The authors interpret this as evidence that late-sighted individuals have developed an over-reliance on chromatic cues for object recognition.
A separate group of 18 Prakash patients, aged 8-20, was tested at multiple post-operative time points beginning two days after surgery.
On each trial two discs were presented, one gray and one carrying a slight hue, and the patient reported which disc appeared colored.
Performance was comparable to that of ten normally sighted controls from the outset, for red, green, and blue stimuli alike, and across variations in luminance and hue disparity.
It is worth being precise about what this establishes and what it does not.
The task indexes chromatic detection with a single psychophysical measure; it does not separately engage the L-M and S-cone pathways, and it was not conducted at equiluminance (Section 4.5).

Converging evidence from a different congenital-cataract population is nonetheless consistent with preserved chromatic function: Pitchaimuthu et al. (2019), testing sight-recovery individuals in Hyderabad on the Farnsworth D-15, found all measured indices of color discrimination unaltered by congenital visual deprivation.
text.formatted: Converging evidence from a different congenital-cataract population is nonetheless consistent with preserved chromatic function: <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Pitchaimuthu et al. (2019)</ref>, testing sight-recovery individuals in Hyderabad on the Farnsworth D-15, found all measured indices of color discrimination unaltered by congenital visual deprivation.

text.text: I therefore accept, for the purposes of this commentary, that the Prakash patients' chromatic discrimination is broadly normal at the onset of post-operative vision.

What does not follow is that each chromatic subsystem has been shown to be independently adult-like, or that the visual system as a whole is mature: post-surgical acuity remains well below normal (Section 4.4).
A note on terminology before describing the simulations.

Throughout this commentary, "training" denotes the supervised optimization of a neural network's weights on a labeled image set -a mathematical operation internal to the model -and never the visual experience of a human observer, for which I use "experience."

The regimen labels introduced here (G2C, C2C, G2G, C2G) name training schedules, not theories; where I refer below to the G2C regimen I mean the specific gray-then-color training schedule, not the developmental hypothesis it is intended to instantiate.

AlexNet (Krizhevsky et al., 2012) was trained on ImageNet (Deng et al., 2009) and FaceScrub (Ng & Winkler, 2014) under four regimens: Gray-to-Color (G2C, intended to mimic normal development), Color-to-Color (C2C, mimicking the Prakash experience), Grayto-Gray (G2G), and Color-to-Gray (C2G, an inverted developmental sequence).
text.formatted: AlexNet <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Krizhevsky et al., 2012)</ref> was trained on ImageNet <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Deng et al., 2009)</ref> and FaceScrub <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Ng & Winkler, 2014)</ref> under four regimens: Gray-to-Color (G2C, intended to mimic normal development), Color-to-Color (C2C, mimicking the Prakash experience), Grayto-Gray (G2G), and Color-to-Gray (C2G, an inverted developmental sequence).

text.text: The G2C network showed generalization across color, grayscale, and hue-rotated stimuli.
The C2C network performed poorly on grayscale and showed strong sensitivity to hue changes.
The C2G network performed poorly overall.
The ordering of experience, not merely its aggregate composition, appears to matter.
The developmental coupling challenge to Vogelsang et al. operates at two levels.

The first concerns the sequencing premise on which the entire account rests: the claim that neonatal color immaturity creates a luminance-first window during which object representations are consolidated before mature chromatic input becomes available.

The coupling evidence reviewed in Sections 3.1 through 3.4 undermines this premise by showing that the same front-end photoreceptor bottleneck constrains color and luminance sensitivity simultaneously, so that no such window exists (Figure 2; Table 1).

text.text: The Vogelsang et al. account requires a luminance-first window: a period during which luminance-based object representations consolidate before mature chromatic input arrives.

The coupling evidence below shows no such window exists, because the bottleneck that degrades color in neonates degrades luminance and spatial processing equally. Teller (1997) synthesized decades of research on infant visual development and argued that the various immaturities of the neonatal visual system are deeply coupled.

text.text: Foveal cone immaturity at birth -coarse packing, short outer segments, and poor waveguide properties (Yuodelis & Hendrickson, 1986; Abramov et al., 1982) -simultaneously limits spatial resolution, contrast sensitivity, and chromatic sensitivity through a shared front-end bottleneck.

text.text: Banks and Bennett (1988) made this quantitative.
Using an ideal observer framework, they showed that neonates' chromatic sensitivity losses are predictable from their luminance sensitivity losses, given the available stimulus gamut.

Their conclusion was that the growth of sensitivity in central red-green and luminance channels must be at least approximately matched during development, or a differential loss in one channel would result -a conclusion Teller (1997) subsequently endorsed in her synthesis of this literature.
text.formatted: Their conclusion was that the growth of sensitivity in central red-green and luminance channels must be at least approximately matched during development, or a differential loss in one channel would result -a conclusion <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Teller (1997)</ref> subsequently endorsed in her synthesis of this literature.

text.text: Color and luminance do not develop independently.
They are yoked.

This coupling operates at the level of absolute sensitivity rather than spectral architecture : Bieber, Volbrecht, and Werner (1995) showed, using VEP-based heterochromatic flicker photometry in 42 infants, that the spectral efficiency function of the luminance channel (the relative weighting of L-and M-cone signals) is already adult-like in early infancy.

text.text: What is immature is how sensitive that channel is, not how it is spectrally tuned.

The luminance pathway thus reaches its adult cone-weighting configuration long before it reaches adult sensitivity levels, while remaining coupled to the chromatic pathway through their shared front-end photoreceptor bottleneck.

The earliest systematic evidence comes from Clavadetscher, Brown, Ankrum, and Teller (1988), who tested 3-and 7-week-olds with forced-choice preferential looking while varying the relative luminance of the two stimuli within each infant.

text.text: Few 3-week-olds made chromatic discriminations; most 7-week-olds did.
The design matters here as much as the result.

Because relative luminance is swept within subject, each infant's performance minimum locates the luminance null, and the same session that demonstrates chromatic discrimination also yields a spectral luminous efficiency function.
The emergence of colour is therefore observed against a concurrently measured luminance function in the same infants, rather than inferred by comparing one literature with another.
The authors attribute much of the performance they observed to rodinitiated signals, which is a further reason not to treat the neonatal chromatic system as an independently maturing module.

The same laboratory had already shown that infant chromatic discrimination depends strongly on stimulus parameters that have nothing to do with the chromatic mechanisms themselves : Packer, Hartmann, and Teller (1984) found Rayleigh discriminations in infants to depend on test field size, so that whether colour vision is detected at a given age is in part a question of how large a stimulus the experimenter chooses. Brown and Teller (1989) then established that chromatic opponent mechanisms are present and functional in 3-month-old infants. Brown, Lindsey, McSweeney, and Walters (1995) then showed that infant color vision is poor not because of any special deficiency in those mechanisms: the culprit is general contrast insensitivity.

That is below every adult value they measured: 0.80 (SE = 0.049) for OKN, 0.81 (SE = 0.038) for direction discrimination and 0.57 (SE = 0.035) for forcedchoice detection.

Expressed relative to luminance contrast sensitivity, infants are as sensitive to color as adults or more so. Allen, Banks, and Norcia (1993) reached the same conclusion from a second laboratory and a different method.

The qualification comes from Dobkins, Anderson, and Lia (1999), who measured chromatic-toluminance sensitivity ratios of 0.82 at three months, 2.42 at four months and 2.91 in adults: at three months the balance is displaced from the adult value by 0.55 log unit, and by four months it has returned to within 0.08. Dobkins, Anderson, and Kelly (2001) found the same sharp gain in chromatic relative to luminance sensitivity between three and four months by a different method, fitting detection contours in L-and M-cone contrast space to the thresholds of 47 infants, and found infant isoluminance points that did not vary with age.

text.text: The coupling claim this commentary makes is not that the balance is invariant at every age, but that no sustained period exists in which luminance is adultlike while color is not.
Brown and colleagues drew the moral themselves: infant color vision is poor because infants are insensitive to contrast, not because of a special immaturity within the color pathways.
This is a common-cause claim, and it should be distinguished from two stronger claims it can be mistaken for.
It is not the claim that chromatic sensitivity reduces to luminance sensitivity, and it is not the claim that either is computed from the other.

It is that a shared front-end limit -immature foveal cone packing, poor optical quality, low effective quantum catch -depresses both measurements at once, so that the two covary across ages and across individuals without either being downstream of the other (Banks & Bennett, 1988). Peterzell, Chang, and Teller (2000) reach the same conclusion from their covariance analysis: in infants, detection thresholds for chromatic and luminance-modulated stimuli "may be limited by common mechanisms," and the covariance channels that are statistically independent in adults are not separable in infants.
text.formatted: It is that a shared front-end limit -immature foveal cone packing, poor optical quality, low effective quantum catch -depresses both measurements at once, so that the two covary across ages and across individuals without either being downstream of the other <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Banks & Bennett, 1988)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Peterzell, Chang, and Teller (2000)</ref> reach the same conclusion from their covariance analysis: in infants, detection thresholds for chromatic and luminance-modulated stimuli "may be limited by common mechanisms," and the covariance channels that are statistically independent in adults are not separable in infants.

text.text: Coupling in development does not imply identity of mechanism; it is two distinct systems maturing under a common constraint.

This conclusion holds most cleanly when infant OKN data are compared to adult 2IFC detection data, reflecting the well-documented difference between detection and direction-discrimination thresholds for chromatic gratings.
What the claim licenses is correspondingly specific.
It does not license the inference, as a matter of logic, that mature color vision entails mature luminance sensitivity.

It licenses an empirical expectation: in the human samples where the two have been measured together, they have been found at comparable stages of maturity, because the structures limiting them are shared.

The Prakash patients are presented as standing outside that regularity, with functionally adult-like color vision at the moment of sight onset, and the burden falls on the account positing the exception to say what makes it possible.
An important objection to this explanation concerns the role of the fovea.

If parafoveal and extrafoveal cones are relatively mature at birth, and VEP and OKN studies use large stimuli that engage the full retina, why should foveal cone immaturity explain coupling across all these conditions?
Several points bear on this question.

Most fundamentally, the coupling argument does not require foveal cone immaturity to be the exclusive bottleneck. Banks and Bennett's (1988) ideal observer analysis accounts for the full retinal mosaic and still predicts that chromatic sensitivity losses are predictable from luminance sensitivity losses given the available signal; the coupling is a property of the front-end signal as a whole, not specifically of foveal optics.
text.formatted: Most fundamentally, the coupling argument does not require foveal cone immaturity to be the exclusive bottleneck. <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Banks and Bennett's (1988)</ref> ideal observer analysis accounts for the full retinal mosaic and still predicts that chromatic sensitivity losses are predictable from luminance sensitivity losses given the available signal; the coupling is a property of the front-end signal as a whole, not specifically of foveal optics.

text.text: Crucially, the empirical coupling evidence was obtained precisely under the conditions the objection identifies as problematic: Brown, Lindsey, McSweeney, and Walters (1995) used large-field OKN stimuli; Dobkins and Teller (1996) used large drifting gratings with free fixation.
text.formatted: Crucially, the empirical coupling evidence was obtained precisely under the conditions the objection identifies as problematic: Brown, Lindsey, McSweeney, and Walters (1995) used large-field OKN stimuli; <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Dobkins and Teller (1996)</ref> used large drifting gratings with free fixation.

text.text: Coupling holds under conditions designed to minimize foveal dominance.

For object recognition specifically, moreover, foveal processing dominates regardless of stimulus size, because observers fixate objects of interest; the developmental story concerns a foveally driven process even when stimuli are large.
Foveal cone immaturity is probably an incomplete account of the full range of neonatal visual limitations; incomplete myelination and cortical immaturity likely contribute.
But mechanistic incompleteness does not undermine the empirical fact of coupling, which is multiply confirmed across methods, laboratories, age ranges, and stimulus conditions.
Complementary electrophysiological evidence comes from VEP studies of infant spatial vision.

An important precursor was Volbrecht and Werner (1987), who used steady-state VECPs to demonstrate that short-wavelength-sensitive cones are present and functional in 4-6-week-old infants, establishing that S-cone pathways exist from the first weeks of life even while remaining immature.

text.text: Crognale, Kelly, Chang, Weiss, and Teller (1997) and Crognale, Kelly, Weiss, and Teller (1998) then used chromatic onset VEPs to trace the development of achromatic and chromatic pathways longitudinally over the first postnatal year.
text.formatted: Crognale, Kelly, Chang, Weiss, and <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Teller (1997)</ref> and Crognale, Kelly, Weiss, and Teller (1998) then used chromatic onset VEPs to trace the development of achromatic and chromatic pathways longitudinally over the first postnatal year.

text.text: Stimuli were modulated along all three axes of a cone-based color space: achromatic (luminance), red-green (L-M), and tritan (Scone), allowing each pathway to be tracked separately.
The result was not a single coupled trajectory but a cascade.

Achromatic VEP responses matured earliest, with latencies decreasing to adult-like values within approximately 12-15 weeks of life, consistent with Bieber, Volbrecht, and Werner's (1995) finding that the spectral tuning of the luminance channel is adult-configured from early infancy, even while absolute sensitivity remains low.
text.formatted: Achromatic VEP responses matured earliest, with latencies decreasing to adult-like values within approximately 12-15 weeks of life, consistent with <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Bieber, Volbrecht, and Werner's (1995)</ref> finding that the spectral tuning of the luminance channel is adult-configured from early infancy, even while absolute sensitivity remains low.

text.text: Chromatic responses appeared later: L-M responses at around 4 weeks and S-cone (tritan) responses at around 6-8 weeks, and both changed continuously throughout the first year of life.

Critically, however, the L-M and S-cone chromatic waveforms were equally immature even at 12 months of age. Madrid and Crognale (2000) extended this developmental picture in a cross-sectional study of subjects from 2 years to adulthood, finding that chromatic VEP waveforms, which shift from a positive-negative to a negative-positive complex with age, do not achieve adult form until after 12-13 years, while achromatic responses to low spatialfrequency reversal stimuli appear adult-like by 1 year of age.

text.text: A broader review of this evidence (Crognale, 2002) concluded that achromatic and chromatic pathways proceed at least partially independently, with chromatic waveforms remaining immature for far longer than their achromatic counterparts.

text.text: Because the stimuli were designed to preferentially activate specific chromatic pathways, the developmental cascade reflects pathway-specific maturation rather than simply summed population-level electrophysiology.

By using equiluminant onset stimuli modulated along cardinal color-space axes, it is possible to preferentially modulate L-M or S-cone pathways and track their separate developmental trajectories (Duncan et al., 2012; Kaneko et al., 2020 Kaneko et al., , 2025;; Emery et al., 2017 Emery et al., , 2023;; Rozman, Racey, & Bosten, 2025).

text.text: That said, it is the convergence of this VEP evidence with the behavioral results of Knoblauch, Vital-Durand, and Barbur (2001) that most firmly establishes a slow, pathway-specific developmental timetable: without that behavioral convergence, changes in the chromatic VEP waveforms over development could in principle have reflected more general maturational processes, such as cortical myelination, rather than chromatic pathway maturation per se.
text.formatted: That said, it is the convergence of this VEP evidence with the behavioral results of <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Knoblauch, Vital-Durand, and Barbur (2001)</ref> that most firmly establishes a slow, pathway-specific developmental timetable: without that behavioral convergence, changes in the chromatic VEP waveforms over development could in principle have reflected more general maturational processes, such as cortical myelination, rather than chromatic pathway maturation per se.

text.text: The two sources of evidence, taken together, rule out that alternative. Boon, Suttle, and Dain (2007) extended this work into childhood.
text.formatted: The two sources of evidence, taken together, rule out that alternative. <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Boon, Suttle, and Dain (2007)</ref> extended this work into childhood.

text.text: Using equiluminant L-M gratings, they measured both VEP and psychophysical chromatic contrast thresholds in children (ages 4.8-12.6 years) and adults, finding that chromatic sensitivity continues to improve through at least early adolescence and that VEP thresholds in children are systematically higher than matched psychophysical thresholds.

This dissociation means that behavioral measures of chromatic sensitivity, including the color detection task used in Experiment 2 of Vogelsang et al., may underestimate residual chromatic neural immaturity.

Boon, Suttle, Henry, and Dain (2009) extended this analysis using nonlinear dynamical methods, finding that children's chromatic VEPs require fewer independent dynamical variables than adults', confirming that chromatic neural processing continues maturing beyond behavioral threshold.
Critically, this immaturity has both retinal and cortical components: retinal function matures first, while cortical chromatic processing continues changing across the entire childhood age range.

Psychophysical data point the same way: specified at the retinal level, the sensitivities of the foveal S-, M-and L-cone mechanisms already decline steadily from age 10 to age 84 (Werner & Steele, 1988), so the chromatic gains that continue into adolescence are unlikely to be receptoral.
text.formatted: Psychophysical data point the same way: specified at the retinal level, the sensitivities of the foveal S-, M-and L-cone mechanisms already decline steadily from age 10 to age 84 <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">(Werner & Steele, 1988)</ref>, so the chromatic gains that continue into adolescence are unlikely to be receptoral.

text.text: If the Prakash patients' chromatic processing is control-like at both retinal and cortical stages within days of surgery, as their performance suggests but does not establish, they are in a condition without precedent at any stage of normal development.
Together, these studies confirm that the chromatic cascade extends well into childhood, with adult-like chromatic processing not established until adolescence.

An independent review reaches the same conclusion from both directions at once. Van den Boomen, van der Smagt, and Kemner (2012), surveying the behavioural and neurophysiological literature on form-characteristic processing from birth to adulthood, place adult-like colour discrimination at around adolescence and the corresponding cortical responses at approximately nineteen years, citing Peterzell, Chang, and Teller (2000) and Knoblauch et al. (2001) among others.
text.formatted: An independent review reaches the same conclusion from both directions at once. <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Van den Boomen, van der Smagt, and Kemner (2012)</ref>, surveying the behavioural and neurophysiological literature on form-characteristic processing from birth to adulthood, place adult-like colour discrimination at around adolescence and the corresponding cortical responses at approximately nineteen years, citing <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Peterzell, Chang, and Teller (2000)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Knoblauch et al. (2001)</ref> among others.

text.text: The same review places luminance contrast sensitivity for low spatial frequencies, the range to which infants are first sensitive, at nine to twelve years behaviourally and eight to eleven years by evoked potential, and concludes that the cortical mechanisms underlying spatial-frequency processing remain immature in children under eleven.

That conjunction is what matters for the present argument, and the chromatic literature alone does not supply it: at the ages at which the Prakash patients gain sight, neither dimension is mature by either measure.
The claim being made here is not that the two run on identical schedules, and that review's own summary is that different mechanisms mature at different rates.
It is that there is no age, and in particular no age in infancy, at which luminance is finished and colour is not.
This cascade has direct bearing on the Vogelsang et al. account.
The neonatal visual system is not simply "color-immature" as a single undifferentiated state.
It involves at least three distinct developmental timelines (achromatic, L-M chromatic, and S-cone chromatic) that unfold in a specific temporal order.
What is known of the Prakash patients is narrower than this structure requires.

Their chromatic discrimination is control-like within days of surgery, but it was assessed with a single task that does not separately engage the L-M and S-cone pathways, so the claim that all three subsystems are independently mature is not established by the available data.

What can be said is that chromatic performance arrives at a control-like level while the luminance system remains conspicuously immature at high spatial frequencies, since postsurgical acuity is far from normal.
That conjunction -chromatic discrimination near control levels alongside markedly subnormal spatial resolution -has no counterpart in normal visual development at any age.
The G2C training regimen, which implements a single binary switch from achromatic to full-color training, captures none of this internal structure.
A neurobiologically faithful account would need to model the cascade of chromatic subsystem maturation, not merely the presence or absence of color as a whole.

Complementary evidence for developmental coupling comes from individual differences research applying a factor-analytic methodology to infant and adult contrast sensitivity data (Peterzell, Werner, & Kaplan, 1993 , 1995; Peterzell, 1991 Peterzell, , 2016;; Peterzell & Teller, 1996; Peterzell & Elliott, 2026).
text.formatted: Complementary evidence for developmental coupling comes from individual differences research applying a factor-analytic methodology to infant and adult contrast sensitivity data <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Peterzell, Werner, & Kaplan, 1993</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Peterzell, 1991</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Peterzell, , 2016;;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Peterzell & Teller, 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Peterzell & Elliott, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: This work asked whether spatial frequency channels shift together during development (the "scale-change hypothesis") or develop independently.

The scale-change hypothesis, as formalized by Wilson (1988 Wilson ( , 1993) ) after a suggestion by Teller (acknowledged in Wilson, 1988), posits that spatial frequency channels in the infant visual system are present from early in life but shift jointly in both sensitivity and spatial scale as development proceeds, rather than each channel growing independently.
text.formatted: The scale-change hypothesis, as formalized by <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">Wilson (1988</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Wilson ( , 1993) )</ref> after a suggestion by Teller (acknowledged in <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">Wilson, 1988)</ref>, posits that spatial frequency channels in the infant visual system are present from early in life but shift jointly in both sensitivity and spatial scale as development proceeds, rather than each channel growing independently.

text.text: Early empirical supports (with similar theories) included Brown, Dobson, and Maier (1987), who measured infant visual acuity across a range of photopic luminance levels and found orderly scaledependent developmental patterns, and Greenlee, Magnussen, and Nordby (1988), who used scotopic adaptation in rod monochromats to estimate spatial channel tuning at low light levels.
text.formatted: Early empirical supports (with similar theories) included <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Brown, Dobson, and Maier (1987)</ref>, who measured infant visual acuity across a range of photopic luminance levels and found orderly scaledependent developmental patterns, and <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Greenlee, Magnussen, and Nordby (1988)</ref>, who used scotopic adaptation in rod monochromats to estimate spatial channel tuning at low light levels.

text.text: The scale-change hypothesis was not uncontested, however. Banks and Crowell (1993), in a chapter re-examining two competing analyses of front-end limitations to infant vision, Wilson's (1988) scale-change model and the Banks and Bennett (1988) ideal observer framework, concluded that the evidence from masking and adaptation paradigms was ambiguous about whether spatial channels in infants genuinely shift their tuning frequencies during development, as opposed to merely changing in sensitivity.

text.text: Traditional group-mean methods could not distinguish these alternatives with confidence.

Psychophysical and VEP studies of infant luminance contrast sensitivity functions (Peterzell, Werner, & Kaplan, 1993 , 1995; Peterzell, 1991 Peterzell, , 2016;; Peterzell & Teller, 1996; Peterzell & Elliott, 2026) demonstrated that individual differences in infants' contrast sensitivity at one spatial frequency were correlated with differences at neighboring frequencies but not at distant ones, a pattern consistent with spatially localized channels.

text.text: Factor analyses revealed factors that shifted in both sensitivity and spatial scale across the age range studied (4 to 8 months), at rates congruent with the Yuodelis and Hendrickson (1986) data on cone spacing and growth, supporting the scale-change model over the alternative in which channels develop independently.

text.text: This psychophysical covariance-channel work was extended to the electrophysiological domain in Peterzell and Kelly (1997), who applied the same individual differences and factor-analytic methodology to sweep-VEP contrast sensitivity functions in adults and in 8-, 14-, 20-, and 32week-old infants.
text.formatted: This psychophysical covariance-channel work was extended to the electrophysiological domain in <ref type="bibr">Peterzell and Kelly (1997)</ref>, who applied the same individual differences and factor-analytic methodology to sweep-VEP contrast sensitivity functions in adults and in 8-, 14-, 20-, and 32week-old infants.

text.text: The VEP covariance channels showed the same developmental scale shift as the psychophysical channels, consistent with Wilson's (1988 Wilson's ( , 1993) ) scale-change model and the anatomical changes, foveal cone migration and eye growth, that drive it.

text.text: This work was then extended to the chromatic domain in collaboration with Teller. Peterzell and Teller (2000) conducted parallel individual differences analyses of red-green chromatic contrast sensitivity in human adults; Peterzell, Chang, and Teller (2000) carried out the same analyses in human infants.
text.formatted: This work was then extended to the chromatic domain in collaboration with Teller. <ref type="bibr">Peterzell and Teller (2000)</ref> conducted parallel individual differences analyses of red-green chromatic contrast sensitivity in human adults; <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Peterzell, Chang, and Teller (2000)</ref> carried out the same analyses in human infants.

text.text: Both studies found spatial-frequency-tuned covariance channels for chromatic as well as luminance gratings: in adults, two luminance channels and one chromatic channel, three in a combined analysis; in infants, one dominant chromatic channel with a second at the highest spatial frequencies tested, and two to three channels when chromatic and luminance gratings were analysed together.
In infants, chromatic and luminance channels shifted upward in spatial scale at similar rates across age, pointing to a common developmental driver for both modalities.

The two studies differ in one respect that bears directly on the present argument: in adults the chromatic and luminance covariance channels are statistically independent, whereas in infants they were not separable -which is what a shared front-end limit on both would predict.

A separate abstract, Peterzell and Teller (1997), directly addressed whether color and luminance sensitivity are served by the same spatial frequency channels, reporting that they are not (the channels are independent across modalities) but that they develop in parallel, consistent with the coupling hypothesis.
text.formatted: A separate abstract, <ref type="bibr">Peterzell and Teller (1997)</ref>, directly addressed whether color and luminance sensitivity are served by the same spatial frequency channels, reporting that they are not (the channels are independent across modalities) but that they develop in parallel, consistent with the coupling hypothesis.

text.text: The separability of chromatic and luminance mechanisms in adults is wellestablished by independent means (Dobkins, Gunther, & Peterzell, 2000), and is not in tension with developmental coupling: it is precisely what the coupling hypothesis predicts, namely that two distinct but jointly immature systems mature together, each remaining its own system.
text.formatted: The separability of chromatic and luminance mechanisms in adults is wellestablished by independent means <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Dobkins, Gunther, & Peterzell, 2000)</ref>, and is not in tension with developmental coupling: it is precisely what the coupling hypothesis predicts, namely that two distinct but jointly immature systems mature together, each remaining its own system.

text.text: Kelly, Borchert, and Teller (1997) measured achromatic and chromatic CSFs with sweepcontrast VEPs across 8 to 32 weeks of age and found closely matched scale shifts in both over development. Peterzell, Kelly, Chang, Gordon, Omaljev, and Teller (1996) and Peterzell, Chang, Kelly, Hartzler, and Teller (1997) applied the covariance-channel methodology to VEP data from adults and from infants at 2, 3.5, 5, and 8 months, finding the same simultaneous chromatic and luminance scale shift observed in the psychophysical data.

text.text: The psychophysical data for temporal contrast sensitivity shows a similar result.

Karen Dobkins, then a postdoctoral researcher in Teller's laboratory, showed directly that infants' motion detection ratios for chromatically-defined and luminance-defined stimuli develop in parallel (Dobkins & Teller, 1996), a result that is only possible if the two sensitivities are tracking each other.
text.formatted: Karen Dobkins, then a postdoctoral researcher in Teller's laboratory, showed directly that infants' motion detection ratios for chromatically-defined and luminance-defined stimuli develop in parallel <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Dobkins & Teller, 1996)</ref>, a result that is only possible if the two sensitivities are tracking each other.

text.text: The motion-nulling technique used in that study had been validated for infant subjects by Teller and Lindsey (1989), who established that infant OKN responses to isochromatic gratings are governed by the same peripheral luminance mechanism as in adults.

text.text: Temporal contrast sensitivity functions for chromatic gratings in 3-month-olds, while differing in shape from adult functions, track the overall developmental trajectory of their luminance counterparts (Dobkins, Lia, & Teller, 1997).
text.formatted: Temporal contrast sensitivity functions for chromatic gratings in 3-month-olds, while differing in shape from adult functions, track the overall developmental trajectory of their luminance counterparts <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Dobkins, Lia, & Teller, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: Dobkins, Anderson, and Lia (1999) measured both chromatic and luminance temporal CSFs in 3-and 4-month-olds.

The luminance tCSF is somewhat closer to adult-like shape earlier than the chromatic tCSF, suggesting the M pathway matures precociously relative to the P pathway -a nuance to the coupling story, not a refutation.
Both functions are immature and developing rapidly within the same window, shifting together rather than independently.

Two additional findings from Dobkins and colleagues bear directly on the Vogelsang et al. results. Dobkins and Anderson (2002) reported that color-based motion processing is stronger in young infants than in adults, a result that complicates the assumption that neonatal color vision is straightforwardly deficient.
text.formatted: Two additional findings from Dobkins and colleagues bear directly on the Vogelsang et al. results. <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Dobkins and Anderson (2002)</ref> reported that color-based motion processing is stronger in young infants than in adults, a result that complicates the assumption that neonatal color vision is straightforwardly deficient.

text.text: Particularly telling is their finding that absolute color-motion performance declined with age during a period over which color sensitivity clearly improved, a dissociation difficult to reconcile with neonatal color immaturity in the way Vogelsang et al. require.

More directly parallel to the Vogelsang et al. design, Bosworth and Dobkins (2009) measured both chromatic and luminance contrast sensitivity in 25 preterm and 77 fullterm infants, groups that differ, like the Prakash patients and controls, in the amount and kind of visual experience they have had at testing.
text.formatted: More directly parallel to the <ref type="bibr">Vogelsang et al. design, Bosworth and Dobkins (2009)</ref> measured both chromatic and luminance contrast sensitivity in 25 preterm and 77 fullterm infants, groups that differ, like the Prakash patients and controls, in the amount and kind of visual experience they have had at testing.

text.text: If early visual experience preferentially boosts one channel, this should manifest as a differential effect of prematurity on chromatic versus luminance sensitivity.
It does.

Luminance sensitivity in their sample was predicted by postterm age, as preprogrammed maturation alone would predict, whereas chromatic sensitivity exceeded that prediction: the preterm infants' additional 6.6 weeks of visual experience was worth roughly 3.7 weeks of chromatic development.
Their conclusion is that chromatic contrast sensitivity is more influenced by early postnatal visual experience than luminance contrast sensitivity is.
This is the closest existing empirical analogue to the Vogelsang et al. design, and it is the strongest published challenge to the coupling argument advanced here.
It should be stated plainly rather than assimilated.
Three considerations nevertheless limit what it licenses.

First, magnitude: the effect is a few weeks of acceleration within the first six months, set against a chromatic trajectory that on the behavioral evidence runs to roughly eighteen years (Knoblauch et al., 2001).
text.formatted: First, magnitude: the effect is a few weeks of acceleration within the first six months, set against a chromatic trajectory that on the behavioral evidence runs to roughly eighteen years <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Knoblauch et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: A rate modulation of that size is not a sensitive period that opens and closes.
Second, applied to the Prakash patients the result cuts the other way.

If chromatic sensitivity depends on early postnatal visual experience more than luminance sensitivity does, then patients who had no patterned visual experience at all before surgery should arrive with chromatic sensitivity lagging, not with a color channel positioned to dominate.
Vogelsang et al. require the patients' color vision to be functionally adult-like at sight onset; the mechanism Bosworth and Dobkins identify predicts that it should not be.
Third, and most important, both channels in their sample remain far from mature across the window studied, and both improve substantially over it.

Their full-term data show this directly (Figure 2d): from 2 to 7 months both sensitivities rise by about 0.7 log unit, while the difference between them stays within 0.2 log unit of zero, with no trend across age.
text.formatted: Their full-term data show this directly (Figure <ref type="figure">2d</ref>): from 2 to 7 months both sensitivities rise by about 0.7 log unit, while the difference between them stays within 0.2 log unit of zero, with no trend across age.

text.text: The preterm effect is a modulation of rate on top of joint immaturity, not a dissociation between a mature channel and an immature one.
The coupling claim this commentary needs is the claim about the magnitude of the two immaturities during infancy, and that claim survives.

Taken together, behavioral, electrophysiological, and individual-differences studies converge on the same conclusion (Table 1): chromatic and luminance sensitivity are coupled through shared photoreceptor immaturity, and no developmental window exists during which luminance-based object representations can form while color is specifically suppressed.
text.formatted: Taken together, behavioral, electrophysiological, and individual-differences studies converge on the same conclusion (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>): chromatic and luminance sensitivity are coupled through shared photoreceptor immaturity, and no developmental window exists during which luminance-based object representations can form while color is specifically suppressed.

text.text: If color and luminance are coupled through shared photoreceptor immaturity -as the foregoing evidence shows -the comparison between Prakash patients and normally sighted infants is more complex than Vogelsang et al. acknowledge.
Vogelsang et al. are themselves aware that Prakash patients differ from neonates in multiple respects, and they acknowledge the limitations of the patient comparison in general terms.
What they do not engage with, however, is the coupling problem specifically.
At the onset of post-operative vision, Prakash patients do not merely have substantially elevated color sensitivity.

By the logic of developmental coupling, they should also have substantially elevated luminance sensitivity, spatial resolution, contrast sensitivity, and temporal processing -all dimensions simultaneously elevated far above neonatal levels, though not yet fully adult (Figure 2c).
text.formatted: By the logic of developmental coupling, they should also have substantially elevated luminance sensitivity, spatial resolution, contrast sensitivity, and temporal processing -all dimensions simultaneously elevated far above neonatal levels, though not yet fully adult (Figure <ref type="figure">2c</ref>).

text.text: This creates a causal identification problem: Vogelsang et al. attribute over-reliance on color to mature color vision at sight onset, but if luminance and spatial processing are equally mature, any or all of these factors could be causal.
As argued in Section 1, the cause may lie in the richness and simultaneity of the input itself rather than in any single one of its dimensions.

As illustrated in Figure 1, panels (b)-(d), this creates a causal identification problem: the developmental condition required by Vogelsang et al. -luminance mature while color lags (panel d) -does not occur in normal human visual development.
text.formatted: As illustrated in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1</ref>, panels (b)-(d), this creates a causal identification problem: the developmental condition required by Vogelsang et al. -luminance mature while color lags (panel d) -does not occur in normal human visual development.

text.text: Vogelsang et al. interpret the color-over-grayscale asymmetry as evidence that patients never built luminance-grounded representations, because they lacked the early color-degraded period that would have forced reliance on luminance structure.

A coupling-consistent account does not dispute the observation but offers a different explanation: the grayscale deficit may reflect the absence of the normal developmental sequence during which object representations form under conditions of simultaneously low spatial resolution, low contrast sensitivity, and degraded color -conditions that together force reliance on coarse luminance structure.
Substantially elevated color sensitivity at sight onset is a marker of the disrupted sequence, not its cause.
The colorspecific framing singles out one strand of what is actually a coordinated developmental disruption.

Teller (1997) characterized the newborn's visual world as defined not only by "the haziness of low-contrast sensitivity" and "the blurriness of spatial filtering" but also by "the blandness of monochrome" (p. 2196).
These three features are not independent; they are co-occurring manifestations of the same foveal immaturity.

The Vogelsang et al. account extracts one strand of this bundle and attributes adaptive significance to it alone, without justifying why color, rather than low spatial resolution or low contrast sensitivity, should be the critical variable (see also Vogelsang et al., 2018).
text.formatted: The Vogelsang et al. account extracts one strand of this bundle and attributes adaptive significance to it alone, without justifying why color, rather than low spatial resolution or low contrast sensitivity, should be the critical variable (see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Vogelsang et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: No known patient population combines mature luminance and spatial processing with immature color vision at sight onset, pointing to a deeper issue: the Vogelsang et al. hypothesis does not specify which aspect of neonatal immaturity is doing the causal work, leaving the account conceptually underdetermined.
The hypothesis that color immaturity specifically is the critical factor cannot be cleanly falsified, because the theoretical machinery does not specify what would count as a test.
One partial exception deserves exploration.

Anomalous trichromats fitted with spectral notch filters show increases in chromatic contrast response that accumulate gradually over roughly two weeks of wear and that persist when the filters are removed, implying postreceptoral plasticity in observers whose spatial and luminance vision is entirely normal (Werner, Marsh-Armstrong, & Knoblauch, 2020).
text.formatted: Anomalous trichromats fitted with spectral notch filters show increases in chromatic contrast response that accumulate gradually over roughly two weeks of wear and that persist when the filters are removed, implying postreceptoral plasticity in observers whose spatial and luminance vision is entirely normal <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">(Werner, Marsh-Armstrong, & Knoblauch, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: This is not a sight-restoration population, and the manipulation enhances chromatic contrast rather than restoring an absent dimension.
It does, however, offer something the sight-restoration literature cannot: a case in which chromatic sensitivity changes substantially while luminance and spatial processing are held fixed.

Testing whether object recognition becomes measurably more color-dependent in such observers would be a tractable, if indirect, probe of whether chromatic availability on its own is sufficient to reshape representational reliance.
The G2C regimen provides only indirect support for the color-specific account, since it manipulates color availability while holding spatial resolution constant.

A more stringent test would degrade color, spatial resolution, and contrast simultaneously in developmentally realistic proportions to determine whether color degradation alone is necessary to reproduce the observed generalization pattern.
>Methodological Concerns
text.formatted: <head n="4." >Methodological Concerns</head>

text.text: Vogelsang et al. have archived the Experiment 1 data (Vogelsang & Vogelsang, 2024), which makes it possible to examine directly how the reported effect depends on the scale on which it is measured.
text.formatted: Vogelsang et al. have archived the Experiment 1 data <ref type="bibr">(Vogelsang & Vogelsang, 2024)</ref>, which makes it possible to examine directly how the reported effect depends on the scale on which it is measured.

text.text: I reanalyzed those data; the results are summarized in Figure 3.
text.formatted: I reanalyzed those data; the results are summarized in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref>.

text.text: The published analysis reproduces exactly.

The color-over-grayscale benefit, computed as the difference in naming accuracy in percentage points, averages 12.70 points in the Prakash group and 2.70 points in controls, and the group difference is reliable, t(18) = 3.501, p = 0.003, d = 1.57 (Figure 3b).
text.formatted: The color-over-grayscale benefit, computed as the difference in naming accuracy in percentage points, averages 12.70 points in the Prakash group and 2.70 points in controls, and the group difference is reliable, t(18) = 3.501, p = 0.003, d = 1.57 (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3b</ref>).

text.text: The difficulty is that the two groups occupy very different regions of the performance scale.

Controls name objects correctly on 90.9% of color trials and 88.2% of grayscale trials, with two of the ten at 100% correct in the color condition; the Prakash patients average 57.7% and 45.0% respectively (Figure 3a).
text.formatted: Controls name objects correctly on 90.9% of color trials and 88.2% of grayscale trials, with two of the ten at 100% correct in the color condition; the Prakash patients average 57.7% and 45.0% respectively (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3a</ref>).

text.text: Percentage-point differences are not comparable across these regions, because a given change in underlying discriminability produces a smaller change in percent correct near the ceiling than near the middle of the range.
The conventional remedy for bounded proportion data is to analyze the effect on a scale on which it is additive, which for proportions is log odds.
On that scale the group difference is not reliable.
The mean benefit is 0.67 log odds in controls and 0.60 log odds in the Prakash patients, t(18) = -0.19, p = 0.85 (Figure 3c).
text.formatted: The mean benefit is 0.67 log odds in controls and 0.60 log odds in the Prakash patients, t(18) = -0.19, p = 0.85 (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3c</ref>).

text.text: The conclusion does not depend on how the two ceiling observations are handled: a Haldane correction, clamping at 0.005 and 0.995, and the Smithson-Verkuilen squeeze yield group × stimulus-type interactions of p = 0.85, p = 0.93 and p = 0.16 respectively, none of them reliable.

Nor does it depend on the specification of the analysis of variance: entering stimulus type as a withinsubjects factor gives F(1,18) = 0.04, p = 0.85, and entering it as a between-subjects factor gives F(1,36) = 0.01, p = 0.92.
A binomial generalized estimating equation fitted at the trial level, with participants as clusters, returns the same answer for the interaction, β = -0.22, p = 0.39.

A default Bayesian two-sample t-test on the benefit scores gives BF₁₀ = 14.4 on the percentage scale but BF₀₁ = 2.5 on the log-odds scale; the latter is not strong evidence for the null, but it is a clear absence of evidence for the effect.
The interaction is the term that matters.

The claim at issue is not that the Prakash patients recognize objects less accurately than controls -they plainly do, and no one disputes it -but that they draw more benefit from color than controls do.
Measured on a scale appropriate to proportions, they do not.
The trial-level model assumes 100 trials per condition.
The published methods do not give the count; 100 is the smallest for which every archived percentage is exact, and no count below 96 fits the archived values even allowing for rounding.
In any case the analyses that do not rest on a trial count, namely the transformed analyses of variance and the ttests on benefit scores, are unaffected.

This conclusion converges with an independent reanalysis by Wallis and Martin (2026), published in the Journal of Robustness Reports, which arrived at it by a different route and without reference to the present commentary. Wallis and Martin (2026) observe that many control participants perform at or near ceiling on the color condition, which compresses performance differences near the boundary of the scale.
text.formatted: This conclusion converges with an independent reanalysis by <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Wallis and Martin (2026)</ref>, published in the Journal of Robustness Reports, which arrived at it by a different route and without reference to the present commentary. <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Wallis and Martin (2026)</ref> observe that many control participants perform at or near ceiling on the color condition, which compresses performance differences near the boundary of the scale.

text.text: A t-test on raw percentage differences treats a 5-percentage-point improvement near 95% as statistically equivalent to the same improvement near 50%, implicitly assuming a linear probability model with normally distributed errors, an assumption inappropriate for bounded proportion data.

Fitting instead a Bayesian generalized mixed-effects model appropriate to these data, they report no evidence that the latesighted patients rely more on color for object recognition than the controls do.

Their own conclusion is appropriately cautious: whether late-sighted individuals rely more on color information, they write, appears to hinge on which modeling approach one views as most appropriate for the underlying data-generating process.

The analyses reported above agree with theirs across every scale-appropriate model I applied, which I take to narrow the range of defensible positions, but the substantive point is theirs: the reported difference is a property of the measurement scale, and the case for a color-specific group difference has not yet been made.
The remainder of this commentary does not depend on any of the foregoing.

The argument developed in Section 3 was deliberately constructed to hold even if the behavioral effect is granted in full: were a color-over-grayscale benefit specific to late-sighted patients to be established in a larger and better-controlled sample, the developmental interpretation placed upon it would still be unsupported, for reasons that have nothing to do with statistics.
I therefore proceed through Sections 4.2 to 4.5 as though the effect were secure.
Readers persuaded by the reanalysis above may treat what follows as addressing a hypothetical; readers who are not may treat it as the substantive case.

The statistical concern is also related to the order confound discussed in Section 4.3: both problems are most acute precisely because the control group performs near ceiling on the color condition, which is the design feature that makes the raw percentage difference measure both statistically fragile and vulnerable to learning artifacts.
The history of sight-restoration research itself supplies a cautionary precedent.

Leffler et al. (2021) identified Cheselden's (1728) canonical patient -a boy of thirteen couched for congenital cataract, long treated as the founding case for claims about what the newly sighted can and cannot perceive -as someone whose case may have been written up in part by Berkeley, whose philosophical prediction it so conveniently confirmed.
A single observer, socially entangled with the theorist, was treated for nearly three centuries as decisive evidence.

The methodological discipline this paper recommends -adequate sample sizes, preregistered hypotheses, independent replication -is precisely what was missing then, and what remains missing in Vogelsang et al.
The primary behavioral finding rests on ten Prakash patients and ten controls.
While the effect size is large (d = 1.566), small samples are known to produce inflated effect size estimates, and the rarity of the population makes replication difficult.
The computational simulations, while suggestive, do not substitute for converging behavioral evidence from additional late-sighted individuals.

This statistical concern is related to one independently raised by Franklin, Konakanchi, and Conway in their Science eLetter: controls performing near ceiling on the color condition compress the measurable range of the color-over-grayscale benefit for that group, making the comparison between patient and control groups particularly sensitive to modeling assumptions. Wallis and Martin's (2026) reanalysis, discussed in Section 4.1, addresses this directly.
text.formatted: This statistical concern is related to one independently raised by Franklin, Konakanchi, and Conway in their Science eLetter: controls performing near ceiling on the color condition compress the measurable range of the color-over-grayscale benefit for that group, making the comparison between patient and control groups particularly sensitive to modeling assumptions. <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Wallis and Martin's (2026)</ref> reanalysis, discussed in Section 4.1, addresses this directly.

text.text: All participants in Experiment 1 named objects first in grayscale and then in full color.
Any learning or priming effect, such as becoming familiar with objects or learning to use form cues in the first session, would inflate color performance for all participants.
Prakash patients, with generally weaker object representations, may be more susceptible to such learning, producing an apparent "color benefit" that is partly artifactual.
A counterbalanced design would be necessary to rule this out; the fixed order was not discussed as a potential confound.

Their account requires not merely that luminance precedes color somewhat, but that the gap is large enough and long enough for luminance-grounded representations to consolidate before chromatic maturity.
That premise is the crux, and it is worth stating precisely how the position defended here differs from theirs, because the difference is easy to miss.
Vogelsang et al. require a developmental period in which color vision cannot contribute to pattern recognition while luminance vision can.

What the literature reviewed in Section 3 actually describes is a period in which both are reduced in contrast sensitivity and spatial resolution together -color somewhat the more degraded of the two, but never absent, and never lagging by the margin their account needs.

The distinction matters: on their account the developmental work is done by the unavailability of one dimension, whereas on the account defended here it is done by the simultaneous impoverishment of all of them, within which luminance is simply the most reliable signal available rather than the only one.
This concern was independently raised by Franklin, Konakanchi, and Conway in a Science eLetter posted on 14 November 2024 (Franklin, Konakanchi, & Conway, 2024).
text.formatted: This concern was independently raised by Franklin, Konakanchi, and Conway in a Science eLetter posted on 14 November 2024 <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Franklin, Konakanchi, & Conway, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: They state directly that patients were worse for grayscale images "which we think is partly because these were presented first."
Vogelsang et al.'s published reply (Vogelsang et al., 2025) argues that "with no feedback provided and no time limit imposed on responses, a strong ordering effect is unlikely."
text.formatted: Vogelsang et al.'s published reply <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Vogelsang et al., 2025)</ref> argues that "with no feedback provided and no time limit imposed on responses, a strong ordering effect is unlikely."

text.text: This is a design argument, not an empirical demonstration.
The confound is mitigated by logic but not eliminated by data, and a counterbalanced replication remains the necessary test.
Franklin et al. also raised a developmental-timing objection: "at birth, both color and object vision are underdeveloped.
And both develop in parallel."
This converges with the coupling argument in Section 3, confirming that no luminance-first window exists.

Vogelsang et al.'s reply concedes that "both color sensitivity and object recognition are immature at birth and develop gradually" -confirming that the time-lag premise is thinner than the original paper implies.
Gradual parallel development is difficult to reconcile with that requirement.
The normally sighted controls wore blur goggles intended to match the Prakash patients' reduced visual acuity.
This is a thoughtful attempt at equating groups, but an imperfect one.

Blur goggles preferentially attenuate high spatial frequencies, leaving low and mid-frequency contrast sensitivity and therefore much of the object-recognition-relevant contrast sensitivity function unmatched between groups.
Beyond acuity, the Prakash patients differ from controls in years of visual experience, neural plasticity, attentional strategies, object familiarity, and many other factors.
Any of these differences could independently account for the differential reliance on color cues without implicating the developmental color hypothesis.

Luminance contrast sensitivity is bandpass while chromatic contrast sensitivity is low-pass (Mullen, 1985), and amblyopia from years of deprivation most severely disrupts the high-spatialfrequency luminance channels that contribute most to object recognition while leaving chromatic channels relatively intact.
text.formatted: Luminance contrast sensitivity is bandpass while chromatic contrast sensitivity is low-pass <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Mullen, 1985)</ref>, and amblyopia from years of deprivation most severely disrupts the high-spatialfrequency luminance channels that contribute most to object recognition while leaving chromatic channels relatively intact.

text.text: Franklin et al.'s Science eLetter proposed a closely related account: color is useful under low acuity generally, and patients with persistently poor post-surgical acuity would continue to benefit from color cues.
On reflection these are better treated as one account than two.

Both hold that the proximal cause of the color benefit is impaired luminance vision rather than a developmental history effect; they differ only in which end of the same asymmetry they emphasize, Franklin et al. noting that color is generally useful when acuity is poor, and the sensory-loss framing noting that in congenital cataract the loss falls specifically on the highspatial-frequency luminance channels while chromatic channels are relatively spared.

I refer to them jointly below as the differential-sensory-loss account. Ellemberg, Lewis, Maurer, et al. (1999) showed that bilateral congenital cataract patients have severely impaired high-spatial-frequency luminance contrast sensitivity and grating acuity after surgery (reductions averaging 1.3 and 0.5 log units) while low and mid-frequency sensitivity remains within normal limits. Pitchaimuthu et al. (2019), testing sight-recovery individuals in Hyderabad -a different congenital-cataract cohort from Project Prakash -found all indices of Farnsworth D-15 color discrimination unaltered by congenital visual deprivation.
text.formatted: I refer to them jointly below as the differential-sensory-loss account. <ref type="bibr">Ellemberg, Lewis, Maurer, et al. (1999)</ref> showed that bilateral congenital cataract patients have severely impaired high-spatial-frequency luminance contrast sensitivity and grating acuity after surgery (reductions averaging 1.3 and 0.5 log units) while low and mid-frequency sensitivity remains within normal limits. <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Pitchaimuthu et al. (2019)</ref>, testing sight-recovery individuals in Hyderabad -a different congenital-cataract cohort from Project Prakash -found all indices of Farnsworth D-15 color discrimination unaltered by congenital visual deprivation.

text.text: Together these findings suggest the color-over-grayscale benefit reflects a differential sensory loss rather than history-dependent over-reliance on color.
The blur goggles equate acuity but not chromatic sensitivity, leaving this confound uncontrolled.

A definitive test requires measuring both functions within the same patients; the differential-sensory-loss account remains an inference across separate cohorts, but one the existing data cannot rule out. Held et al. (2011) showed that newly sighted individuals fail cross-modal object transfer immediately after surgery but acquire it within days, suggesting the visual system is not locked in a fixed developmental state at the time of testing.
