(2011)</ref> showed that newly sighted individuals fail cross-modal object transfer immediately after surgery but acquire it within days, suggesting the visual system is not locked in a fixed developmental state at the time of testing.

text.text: If the color-dependence pattern reflected a permanent developmental history effect rather than a transient sensory asymmetry, it should persist as other visual capacities are acquired; longitudinal follow-up of the Prakash cohort would be the necessary test.
The G2C network undergoes a sharp transition from all-grayscale to all-color training at the halfway point of the training sequence.

Normal visual development involves a gradual, continuous maturation of chromatic sensitivity over the first several months of postnatal life (Teller, 1998; Skelton, Maule, & Franklin, 2022), not a discrete switch.
text.formatted: Normal visual development involves a gradual, continuous maturation of chromatic sensitivity over the first several months of postnatal life <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(Teller, 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Skelton, Maule, & Franklin, 2022)</ref>, not a discrete switch.

text.text: The specific 50/50 split in training is arbitrary.
More fundamentally, the G2C regimen only degrades color information.
It does not degrade spatial resolution, luminance contrast, or temporal sensitivity, which are equally characteristic of neonatal vision.
Temporal contrast sensitivity also undergoes dramatic developmental change over the first postnatal months (Rasengane, Allen, & Manny, 1997), which the G2C regimen does not address.
text.formatted: Temporal contrast sensitivity also undergoes dramatic developmental change over the first postnatal months <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Rasengane, Allen, & Manny, 1997)</ref>, which the G2C regimen does not address.

text.text: A more biomimetic model would gradually increase chromatic content across the training period and simultaneously degrade spatial resolution, luminance contrast, and temporal sensitivity in a manner consistent with the known developmental trajectory of foveal cone maturation.
A further concern applies to Experiment 2, which was designed to establish that Prakash patients have mature chromatic sensitivity at the onset of post-operative vision.
The task presented pairs of discs, one gray and one colored, and asked which disc appeared colored.
The supplementary material (Table S3) reports the luminances of the stimuli: at full saturation, red, green, and blue discs produced approximately 49, 144, and 15 cd/m² respectively.
text.formatted: The supplementary material (Table <ref type="table">S3</ref>) reports the luminances of the stimuli: at full saturation, red, green, and blue discs produced approximately 49, 144, and 15 cd/m² respectively.

text.text: These values differ dramatically from each other and from the comparison gray.
The task was not conducted at equiluminance.
A patient with functioning luminance contrast sensitivity but impaired chromatic opponency could, in principle, perform above chance by detecting brightness differences rather than hue.

Since coupling predicts that Prakash patients should arrive with substantially elevated luminance contrast sensitivity as well as substantially elevated color sensitivity, performance on a non-equiluminant chromatic discrimination task cannot cleanly establish which capacity is doing the work.
This is not merely a theoretical possibility.
The Experiment 2 data are public (Vogelsang & Vogelsang, 2024) and include performance broken down by the luminance of the chromatic probe.
text.formatted: The Experiment 2 data are public <ref type="bibr">(Vogelsang & Vogelsang, 2024)</ref> and include performance broken down by the luminance of the chromatic probe.

text.text: Pooling across all 51 Prakash testing sessions, detection accuracy varies systematically with probe luminance: 75.3% correct for low-luminance probes, 76.0% for mid-luminance probes, and 68.2% for highluminance probes (Friedman χ²(2) = 16.88, p = 0.0002; low versus high, t(50) = 5.06, p < 0.0001).

text.text: The same pattern is independently reliable at the first post-operative session (p = 0.039) and the second (p = 0.020).
If the task isolated chromatic mechanisms, the luminance of the probe should be largely irrelevant to performance.

That it is not indicates that luminance information contributes to the judgment, and that Experiment 2 therefore does not establish what it is taken to establish: that these patients possess mature chromatic sensitivity specifically, as distinct from an ability to detect the probe by whatever cue is available.
The measurements reported by Vogelsang et al. (2024) are not in dispute here.

text.text: Wallis and Martin (2026) reach a compatible conclusion by an independent route.

The central argument of this commentary is nonetheless directed at the theoretical interpretation rather than at the observation: a recognition benefit for color over grayscale images that is specific to late-sighted patients may yet prove robust in a larger and better-controlled study.

If it did, a simpler explanation would be available, a differential sensory one: Ellemberg, Lewis, Maurer, et al. (1999) and Pitchaimuthu et al. (2019) together suggest that high-spatial-frequency luminance vision is severely impaired in congenital cataract patients while chromatic discrimination is preserved, a sensory asymmetry that would favor color recognition without requiring any developmental-experience mechanism.

(1999)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Pitchaimuthu et al. (2019)</ref> together suggest that high-spatial-frequency luminance vision is severely impaired in congenital cataract patients while chromatic discrimination is preserved, a sensory asymmetry that would favor color recognition without requiring any developmental-experience mechanism.

text.text: The present critique argues that the current evidence does not support the color-developmental interpretation; it does not argue that the underlying observation is false.
What is in dispute is the mechanism.

Vogelsang et al. propose that color-specific developmental experience (the period of neonatal color immaturity that normally forces the visual system to build luminance-grounded object representations) is the critical adaptive variable.
That account treats color immaturity as separable from the broader bundle of neonatal visual immaturities.
The evidence reviewed here shows that it is not.

The evidence reviewed in Sections 3.1 through 3.4 converges on the same conclusion: the neonatal visual system is not merely color-impoverished but globally impoverished, and these immaturities are coupled rather than separable.

The Prakash patients, by contrast, receive chromatic, luminance and spatial information all at once at sight onset, with chromatic discrimination already control-like while spatial vision remains far from normal, a conjunction without counterpart at any stage of normal visual development. Bosworth and Dobkins's (2009) preterm study qualifies this picture in one respect, in showing chromatic sensitivity to be the more experience-sensitive of the two, but it does so within a regime in which both channels remain grossly immature (Section 3.4).
text.formatted: The Prakash patients, by contrast, receive chromatic, luminance and spatial information all at once at sight onset, with chromatic discrimination already control-like while spatial vision remains far from normal, a conjunction without counterpart at any stage of normal visual development. <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Bosworth and Dobkins's (2009)</ref> preterm study qualifies this picture in one respect, in showing chromatic sensitivity to be the more experience-sensitive of the two, but it does so within a regime in which both channels remain grossly immature (Section 3.4).

text.text: The coupling argument more effectively critiques the color-specific account than explains the behavioral pattern.

It shows that substantially elevated color sensitivity at sight onset marks a disrupted developmental sequence rather than an independent causal variable, and that the grayscale deficit may reflect the absence of the entire bundle of early neonatal immaturities rather than color degradation alone.
What it does not yet specify is a precise mechanism linking the disrupted sequence to the recognition performance pattern.
That is the task of the companion paper (Peterzell, 2026).
text.formatted: That is the task of the companion paper <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Peterzell, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: A positive alternative account, developed in a companion paper (Peterzell, 2026), proposes a two-stage developmental scaffolding model in which prenatal retinal activity, including spontaneous retinal waves, establishes the foundational architecture of early visual pathways before any visual experience occurs, and the globally degraded postnatal visual signal then forces the first object representations to be built on luminance structure, the most reliable available signal under conditions of maximal photoreceptor immaturity.
text.formatted: A positive alternative account, developed in a companion paper <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Peterzell, 2026)</ref>, proposes a two-stage developmental scaffolding model in which prenatal retinal activity, including spontaneous retinal waves, establishes the foundational architecture of early visual pathways before any visual experience occurs, and the globally degraded postnatal visual signal then forces the first object representations to be built on luminance structure, the most reliable available signal under conditions of maximal photoreceptor immaturity.

text.text: On that account, the Prakash patients have the prenatal developmental foundation but were deprived of the years of globally impoverished visual experience through which normally developing infants build luminancegrounded object representations.

That paper addresses what the present critique leaves open, namely the question of what positive mechanism would link the disrupted developmental sequence to the specific pattern of recognition performance observed.
One further framing deserves comment, since it has given the color-specific account wider currency than the data support.

In the Perspective accompanying Vogelsang et al., Mamassian (2024) generalized the result into a claim that multistage maturation optimizes vision: perceptual systems are complex, and maturing in stages -motion before color, for instance -is held to serve function better than maturing all at once.
text.formatted: In the Perspective accompanying <ref type="bibr">Vogelsang et al., Mamassian (2024)</ref> generalized the result into a claim that multistage maturation optimizes vision: perceptual systems are complex, and maturing in stages -motion before color, for instance -is held to serve function better than maturing all at once.

text.text: Two difficulties attend this.
The first is evidentiary.

The Perspective's original statement of the finding was inverted, and a published erratum concedes that it misrepresented the results by reporting that late-sighted individuals were poorer with color images than with black-and-white ones, when the observed pattern was the reverse (Mamassian, 2024, and erratum).
text.formatted: The Perspective's original statement of the finding was inverted, and a published erratum concedes that it misrepresented the results by reporting that late-sighted individuals were poorer with color images than with black-and-white ones, when the observed pattern was the reverse <ref type="bibr">(Mamassian, 2024, and erratum)</ref>.

text.text: The second difficulty is mechanistic, and it applies equally to Vogelsang et al.'s own suggestion that early limitations in color perception may be adaptive and advantageous.

Selection can act on correlated developmental traits, but coupling constrains how independently their timing could have been modified, and a sequence in which color specifically is delayed would require variation that delays color alone.

The coupling evidence reviewed in Section 3 provides no evidence of such variation: the same photoreceptor immaturity that degrades chromatic sensitivity degrades luminance and spatial sensitivity along with it, so there is no known developmental mechanism by which color alone could have been delayed while luminance was preserved, and therefore no demonstrated color-specific target for selection.
Staged maturation may well be functionally consequential.
What the developmental physiology does not license is the inference that the staging of color specifically was arranged because it is advantageous.

Future work in this area would benefit from explicit engagement with the coupling literature; from computational models that simultaneously degrade color, spatial resolution, and contrast in developmentally realistic proportions; from counterbalanced behavioral designs; and from converging evidence across larger samples or related patient populations.
The fundamental question Vogelsang et al. have raised, whether early perceptual limitations are adaptive rather than merely incidental, is an important one.
The answer is likely to be more nuanced than a story about color alone.

By reporting a group difference that does not survive transformation to a scale appropriate for bounded proportion data, by not counterbalancing their primary task, by testing chromatic sensitivity with stimuli that were not equiluminant and on which performance demonstrably varies with probe luminance, by resting their theoretical edifice on ten participants, by modeling normal visual development as a binary switch rather than a gradual cascade, and, most critically, by building a color-specific developmental account without engaging with the decades of published evidence showing that color and luminance sensitivity are coupled through the same photoreceptor immaturity, Vogelsang et al. have produced a study whose central claim cannot bear the weight placed on it.
Each of these problems alone would require serious qualification; together, they leave the paper's central theoretical contribution in need of stronger empirical and mechanistic foundations.

text.text: The developmental literature does not merely fail to support the luminance-first hypothesis; it predicts the opposite.

Because color and luminance mature together through a shared front-end bottleneck, the developmental sequence required by Vogelsang et al.'s account cannot occur under normal human visual development.
